meta.title: Marketing and Mind Control 营销心理学

blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 3

Read the passage and answer Questions 27–40.

Marketing and Mind Control

How marketing and advertising appeal to the associative nature of the brain

While there had been a long tradition of giving rings as a commitment to marry, the custom of giving diamond engagement rings was in large part manufactured by one of the most effective marketing campaigns in history. In the early 1900s, diamond sales were declining, posing a serious problem for the company that essentially had control over the diamond market. In 1938, this company hired an advertising agency, which proposed reshaping social attitudes toward diamonds. As well as magazines showing film stars draped in diamonds, the agency arranged for movies to incorporate diamond engagement rings into their plots. The campaign culminated with the slogan: ‘A diamond is forever.’

At the time, the approach was unique. Rather than pushing a brand, the objective was to promote diamonds as the symbol of everlasting love. This was achieved by exploiting the associative nature of the brain: associating neurons¹ activated by the concept of ‘love’ with neurons that encoded the concept of ‘diamonds’. By 1941, diamond sales had increased by 55%.

Advertising comes in many forms, from blatant neon signs to subtly embedded products in movies. In each case, the goal is to mould our habits, desires and opinions. Our visual system is targeted by an avalanche of information on the internet, street posters, billboards and in movie theatres. Our auditory system submits to catchy radio jingles and telemarketers. More surreptitiously, our olfactory system is targeted by variations of vanilla and citrus perfumes aimed at enticing us to linger in a retail outlet.

It is difficult to measure how effective these campaigns are, but as in the ‘A diamond is forever’ campaign, they can be so successful that they change the fabric of our culture. In the case of bottled water, we are swayed by advertising into paying for something that we can obtain for free. Most people cannot distinguish bottled from tap water, much less between brands of bottled water, which is why you rarely hear of a bottled water company proposing a blind taste test.

So why is marketing such an effective mind-control technique? It is interesting to consider whether other animals exhibit anything analogous to humans’ susceptibility to advertising. If we provide a lab rat with two types of cereal, it will consume approximately the same amount of each. However, if we put that rat with another rat that spent its day eating just one type, when faced with a choice, our rat will now show a preference for the same type as the other rat was eating. Psychologists call this ‘socially transmitted food preference’.

What many regard as the first documented examples of cultural learning in primates started with a clever monkey that lived in a colony of Japanese monkeys on the island of Koshima. She began taking her dirt-covered sweet potatoes to the river to wash them before eating them. Upon seeing this, a few other open-minded monkeys picked up on the idea. Potato washing then spread from monkey to monkey and, over the course of a few years, most monkeys were eating clean potatoes. Humans are clearly not the only animals to engage in imitation and social learning.

Learning by observation can be an extraordinarily valuable brain feature. This is how we learn to communicate and perform motor skills as well as deal with many everyday problems. For example, a newcomer struggling to purchase tickets and navigate the subway system in a foreign city may step back to learn from the people nearby. Humans and other primates exhibit multiple forms of imitative learning and this is called cultural transmission.

A component of advertising relies on the marketer’s ability to tap into the brain’s propensity for imitation. Anybody who has watched TV knows advertisements are disproportionately populated with attractive, successful-looking individuals. If we are going to imitate someone, we are more inclined to imitate those who appear to be popular and appealing.

Although not all researchers are convinced by the findings, a number of studies indicate that some animals also imitate dominant members of their group. Primatologist Frans de Waal provides anecdotal evidence of preferential imitation among chimpanzees. He noted that in one particular group the dominant male was hurt and was limping as a result. Soon juvenile males of the group started imitating his limp, a form of flattery that would have been unlikely if a non-dominant male had been injured.

Imitation is undoubtedly an invaluable ability, but often our propensity to imitate generalises indiscriminately, leading to poor decisions. When athlete Dick Fosbury revolutionised the high jump by jumping over the bar backward in 1968, imitators obviously copied his jumping style, not his brand of sports shoes. However, today, sportspeople appear in advertisements asking us to buy the laptops or sports drinks that they promote. Rationally, we know these people’s success did not depend on these products, so it seems our propensity to purchase products relates more to neural programs that evolved to encourage imitation of those further up the social ladder.

Today, companies engage in stealth marketing campaigns in which people are paid to frequent bars or websites to covertly promote certain products. Companies also perform studies in which they track the eye movements of people viewing displays, and carefully craft names, packages and jingles associated with their products.

While we may like to believe that manipulation on a grand scale would not be possible, that’s not to say that advertising is innately harmful. To the contrary, the marketing of products or ideas is essential to human culture. The point is that we should ensure our choices reflect our actual goals and desires, and we must distinguish between the dissemination of information which is for our own good, and our manipulation for the benefit of companies.

¹ neurons: impulse-conducting cells that are the functional units of the nervous system

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Questions 27–31

Choose the correct answer.

27 According to the writer, which marketing technique attempts to make consumers stay in a shop for longer?

28 The writer mentions bottled water in order to show that

29 According to the writer, socially transmitted food preference occurs when

30 According to the writer, how is learning by observation and imitation a useful feature of the brain?

31 According to the writer, how does television advertising exploit the human tendency to imitate others?

Questions 32–36

Choose YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, choose NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, or choose NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

32 The diamond campaign worked by making a connection in people’s minds between diamonds and luxury.

33 People are more aware of visual marketing than auditory marketing.

34 The campaign advertising diamonds had a positive influence on society.

35 There is still some uncertainty about whether animals copy the behaviour of the most powerful animals among them.

36 Consumers make a logical connection between celebrities’ achievements and the products they promote.

Questions 37–40

Complete each sentence with the correct ending. Choose the correct answer and move it into the gap.

Sentence Endings

37 The behaviour of the monkeys on the island of Koshima showed that

38 Primatologist Frans de Waal found that

39 Dick Fosbury is mentioned in order to show that

40 A feature of some modern marketing campaigns is that

A. people imitated behaviour that was linked with success.
B. younger animals of a certain species are more likely to imitate each other.
C. an animal would imitate another that had higher status.
D. imitation of popular sportspeople has occurred for many decades.
E. products are marketed to potential consumers who are unaware that marketing is occurring.
F. animals can develop new habits by observation.
G. incentives are provided for consumers who behave in a certain way.

items.text:
题目翻译：根据作者的说法，哪种营销手段试图让消费者在店内停留更久？
答案：B
解析：原文在讨论嗅觉营销时指出，香草和柑橘香味旨在 enticing us to linger in a retail outlet，即吸引我们在商店里多停留。因此，“散发令人愉悦的气味”对应这一手段，选 B。广播广告歌和海报分别出现在听觉、视觉营销的例子中，但作者没有说它们能延长店内停留时间；店内广播通知则没有提及。
定位：正文第3段
vanilla and citrus perfumes aimed at enticing us to linger
原文翻译：旨在诱使我们停留更久的香草和柑橘香味

题目翻译：作者提到瓶装水，是为了说明什么？
答案：A
解析：作者提到瓶装水，是为了说明广告能影响购买决定：人们会花钱买本可以免费获得的东西，因此选 A。B 把“分不清瓶装水与自来水”换成了“水没有味道”，原文没有这样说。C 把“很少有公司提议盲测”改成“营销活动有效时无须测试”，增加了原文没有的条件和结论。D 则增加了“测试已经证明”，原文并未报告这样的测试。
定位：正文第4段
we are swayed by advertising into paying for something that we can obtain for free
原文翻译：广告诱导我们花钱购买本可免费获得的东西

题目翻译：根据作者的说法，“经由同类传递的食物偏好”会在什么情况下出现？
答案：C
解析：实验鼠原本吃两种谷物的量差不多；与另一只当天只吃一种谷物的鼠待在一起后，它也偏爱那一种。这说明同类的饮食能影响其食物偏好，因此选 C。A 把影响者限定为占支配地位的成员，原文没有这个限制。B 说同类动物天生偏好相同，但实验鼠的偏好是在与另一只鼠相处后才发生变化的。D 则把偏好归因于食物稀缺，原文并未涉及稀缺。
定位：正文第5段
However, if we put that rat with another rat that spent its day eating just one type, when faced with a choice, our rat will now show a preference for the same type as the other rat was eating.
原文翻译：然而，如果把这只鼠与另一只当天只吃过一种谷物的鼠放在一起，那么再次面对选择时，前一只鼠就会偏爱另一只鼠所吃的那种谷物。

题目翻译：根据作者的说法，大脑通过观察和模仿来学习的能力，为什么有用？
答案：A
解析：原文说观察学习能帮助人们 deal with many everyday problems，并举例说明：初到外国城市的人可以向旁人学习买票和搭乘地铁。这对应 A 的 overcome challenges，即克服困难。C 虽然也提到交流，但原文只说“学会交流”，没有说这种能力能让人在与他人交流时获得优势。B 的积极榜样以及 D 的文化规范、人际关系，都不是本段指出的作用。
定位：正文第7段
deal with many everyday problems
原文翻译：应对许多日常问题

题目翻译：根据作者的说法，电视广告如何利用人类模仿他人的倾向？
答案：B
解析：广告中有吸引力、看起来很成功的人物所占比例格外高，而人们更愿意模仿受欢迎、有魅力的人。电视广告正是利用这种倾向，让形象令人向往的人出镜，因此选 B。A 所说的展示购买行为、C 所说的青少年仰慕年长者，原文均未提及。D 则声称代言产品促成了这些人的成功；后文恰恰指出，他们的成功并不依赖这些产品。
定位：正文第8段
attractive, successful-looking individuals
原文翻译：有吸引力、看起来成功的人

items.text:
题目翻译：钻石营销活动通过在人们心中建立钻石与奢华之间的联系而奏效。
答案：NO
解析：题干说钻石营销建立的是钻石与 luxury（奢华）的联系，原文却明确说要把钻石宣传为 everlasting love（永恒爱情）的象征，让大脑把“钻石”与“爱情”联系起来。题干换掉了核心联系对象，与作者的说明不符，因此为 NO。影星佩戴钻石只是宣传手段，不能据此把营销目标理解为奢华。
定位：正文第2段
promote diamonds as the symbol of everlasting love
原文翻译：把钻石宣传为永恒爱情的象征

题目翻译：相比听觉营销，人们更能意识到视觉营销。
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：相关段落分别介绍了视觉、听觉和嗅觉营销，却没有比较人们对视觉与听觉营销的觉察程度。视觉信息量大，并不等于人们更容易察觉；后面的 more surreptitiously（更隐蔽）说的是嗅觉营销，也不能用来判断视觉与听觉哪一种更容易被察觉。因此为 NOT GIVEN。
定位：正文第3段
Our visual system is targeted by an avalanche of information on the internet, street posters, billboards and in movie theatres. Our auditory system submits to catchy radio jingles and telemarketers
原文翻译：互联网、街头海报、广告牌和电影院中的海量信息都以我们的视觉系统为目标；朗朗上口的广播广告歌和电话推销则作用于我们的听觉系统

题目翻译：宣传钻石的营销活动对社会产生了积极影响。
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：作者说钻石营销活动很成功，甚至可能改变我们的文化面貌，但并未评价它对社会的影响是积极还是消极。“销量增加”或“营销成功”不等于“对社会有益”，因此为 NOT GIVEN。结尾对营销总体价值的肯定，也不等于评价这场钻石活动有益。
定位：正文第4段
they can be so successful that they change the fabric of our culture
原文翻译：它们可能成功到足以改变我们的文化面貌

题目翻译：动物是否会模仿群体中最强势成员的行为，仍存在一些不确定性。
答案：YES
解析：虽然有研究表明，一些动物会模仿群体中占支配地位的成员，但作者同时强调 not all researchers are convinced，即并非所有研究人员都信服这些发现。这说明结论仍有争议，对应题干的“仍存在一些不确定性”，因此为 YES。
定位：正文第9段
Although not all researchers are convinced by the findings, a number of studies indicate that some animals also imitate dominant members of their group.
原文翻译：虽然并非所有研究人员都信服这些发现，但多项研究表明，一些动物也会模仿群体中占支配地位的成员。

题目翻译：消费者在名人的成就与他们推广的产品之间建立了合乎逻辑的联系。
答案：NO
解析：作者明确说，从理性上看，我们知道名人的成功并不依赖他们推广的产品；购买倾向似乎更多地来自模仿社会地位较高者的神经机制。题干却说消费者在名人成就与产品之间建立了合乎逻辑的联系，与作者的观点相反，因此为 NO。
定位：正文第10段
Rationally, we know these people’s success did not depend on these products
原文翻译：理性上，我们知道这些人的成功并不依赖这些产品

items.text:
题目翻译：Koshima 岛上猴子的行为表明，______。
答案：F
解析：Koshima 岛的猴子看到同伴把红薯洗净后再吃，便学会了这一做法；随后，洗红薯的习惯在猴群中传播。这说明动物能够通过观察养成新习惯，因此选 F。段落没有把这种模仿限定为年幼同伴之间，也没有讨论奖励或社会地位。
定位：正文第6段
Potato washing then spread from monkey to monkey
原文翻译：随后，洗红薯的做法在猴群中一只传给另一只

题目翻译：灵长类动物学家 Frans de Waal 发现，______。
答案：C
解析：Frans de Waal 观察到，一只占支配地位的雄性黑猩猩受伤后跛行，群体中的年幼雄性随后开始模仿它。作者还指出，如果受伤者不占支配地位，这种模仿就不太可能出现。因此，例子的重点是动物会模仿地位更高者，选 C。B 说的是较年轻的动物相互模仿，与这里强调的模仿对象不同。
定位：正文第9段
He noted that in one particular group the dominant male was hurt and was limping as a result. Soon juvenile males of the group started imitating his limp, a form of flattery that would have been unlikely if a non-dominant male had been injured.
原文翻译：他注意到，在某个群体中，占支配地位的雄性黑猩猩受了伤，因此走路一瘸一拐。不久，群体中的年幼雄性便开始模仿它跛行；这是一种讨好行为，如果受伤的是一只不占支配地位的雄性，就不太可能出现这种情况。

题目翻译：文中提到 Dick Fosbury，是为了说明______。
答案：A
解析：Dick Fosbury 用背向横杆的动作革新了跳高技术，其他人模仿的是他的跳高动作，而非他的运动鞋品牌。作者借此说明，人们模仿的是与成功真正有关的行为，因此选 A。年份只是例子的背景，并不是为了说明人们模仿运动员已经有多久。
定位：正文第10段
imitators obviously copied his jumping style, not his brand of sports shoes
原文翻译：模仿者显然学的是他的跳高动作，而不是他穿的运动鞋品牌

题目翻译：某些现代营销活动的一个特点是，______。
答案：E
解析：一些公司付钱雇人光顾酒吧或访问网站，暗中推广产品。covertly promote 就是“暗中推广”的意思。这里的隐性营销，是在潜在消费者没有意识到营销正在发生的情况下推广产品，因此选 E。拿到报酬的是受雇推广的人，不是因采取某种行为而获得奖励的消费者，所以不能选 G。
定位：正文第11段
stealth marketing campaigns in which people are paid to frequent bars or websites to covertly promote certain products
原文翻译：在隐性营销活动中，人们受雇经常光顾酒吧或访问网站，暗中推广某些产品
